newsitem.title: USA: Exchange leaders remain committed to open outcry.
newsitem.headline: Exchange leaders remain committed to open outcry.

text.p: Leaders from futures exchanges around the world said they were committed to open outcry trade, even as exchange alliances and proposals to link markets have forced a greater emphasis on electronic trading.

"We want to stay with open outcry, because it is a bigger concern for the time being in our business," Gerard Pfauwadel, chairman of Marche A Terme International de France (MATIF), said. "There is no reason to leave the floor and choose only the computer."

Pfauwadel, who was speaking at the Futures Industry Association's (FIA) annual conference here, also said that while GLOBEX, the electronic after-hours trading link between MATIF and the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME), was cheap and efficient, the system was not "a complete success."
He said MATIF and CME members were the system's primary users and that other participants amounted to only about one to two percent of total GLOBEX volume.
MATIF, the CME and Reuters Holdings Plc are members of GLOBEX.
Jack Wigglesworth, chairman of the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE), said LIFFE's emphasis on open outcry stemmed in part from their decision not to join GLOBEX.
"Part of our strategy is from the fact we didn't join GLOBEX," Wigglesworth said. "We think open outcry still is the best platform for trading large-volume products."
However, the CBOT and CME exchanges, whose membership remains wedded to open outcry, have seen greater participation on their respective electronic trading systems, Project A and GLOBEX.

"We think this is going to be a tremendous test," CBOT president Thomas Donovan said, referring to the CBOT's dual commitment to Project A and a new trading floor, which will be opened in February 1997.
In addition, both exchanges will soon have a common interface to TOPS, Trade Order Processing Systems, which will allow orders to be routed to either trading floors from a variety of trading systems.
"I would expect a year from now a lot of things will have to change," CME president Bill Brodsky, said, adding that electronic trading was still in an experimental stage.
Leo Melamed, CME chairman emeritus who moderated the panel discussion and is an outspoken advocate for electronic trading, said, however, it was unnecessary to "shut the lights" on floor trade.
"I believe the best role for electronic trade is as an experimental laboratory for new contracts because you cannot possibly list all contracts on a trading floor," Melamed said.
